title: A Critique of "Scattered-Mind Buddha-Recitation Can Bring Rebirth"
author: Zhanran
excerpt: An essay titled "Scattered-Mind Buddha-Recitation Can Bring Rebirth" has been circulating online. Since it touches on questions of deep concern to many students of the Pure Land school, I will examine and assess it point by point below:

inline.s: An essay titled "Scattered-Mind Buddha-Recitation Can Bring Rebirth" has been circulating on the internet. Because it raises questions of deep concern to many students of the Pure Land school, I will examine and assess it point by point below:
[Commentary] The core question in Pure Land practice is:
the principle of rebirth
— namely, how one may attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
What, then, is the principle of rebirth? The principle of rebirth is this:
Right mindfulness at the moment of death, and the Buddha responds and comes to welcome.
(For details, see
The Principle of Rebirth
.) Therefore both Great Master Tanluan and Great Master Daochuo taught:
Ten continuous thoughts at the point of death, and rebirth is attained.
(For details, see
Great Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teachings
Great Master Daochuo's Instructions on Pure Practice
) Moreover, in the Collection of Peace and Bliss, Great Master Daochuo clearly explained the meaning of the eighteenth vow (Amitābha's original vow):
"If there are sentient beings who, though they have committed evil their whole lives,
at the end of their lives, with ten continuous thoughts, call my name,
and if they are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Here Great Master Daochuo gives a precise explanation of the meaning of "even to ten thoughts" in the eighteenth vow:
At the end of life, with ten continuous thoughts, calling my name.

Therefore in one's daily practice one must earnestly make ten continuous thoughts a settled habit, so as to ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Thus Great Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
"Precisely because calling the name is easy
(because reciting the name is easier than visualization-recitation)
, one is reborn as soon as the recitation continues unbroken
(at the moment of death, provided that the thought of Buddha-recitation continues without being interrupted by deluded thoughts, one attains rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
. If one can keep thought following thought without interruption, making this a lifetime commitment,
(one who practices thus for the whole of this life)
, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn."
(For details, see
The Eighteenth Vow
Ten Thoughts at the Moment of Death: Continued, and One Is Reborn
Great Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
[Right mindfulness at the moment of death, and the Buddha responds and comes to welcome] At the end of life, maintaining
the
right mindfulness of Buddha-recitation, one resonates with the Buddha, and the Buddha comes to guide one onward. Thus Great Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
"Precisely because calling the name is easy
(because reciting the name is easier than visualization-recitation)
, one is reborn as soon as the recitation continues unbroken
(at the moment of death, provided that the thought of Buddha-recitation continues without being interrupted by deluded thoughts, one attains rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
. If one can keep thought following thought without interruption, making this a lifetime commitment,
(one who practices thus for the whole of this life)
, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn."
Both Great Master Tanluan and Great Master Daochuo taught:
Ten continuous thoughts at the point of death, and rebirth is attained.
(For details, see
Great Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
Great Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teachings
Great Master Daochuo's Instructions on Pure Practice
)[Resonance between the responsive and the sacred] The sentient being's aspiration and Amitābha Buddha's response meet and interpenetrate each other.

[Making it a settled habit] Through constant, repeated practice, ten continuous thoughts become second nature. [Scattered-mind Buddha-recitation] Reciting the Buddha's name while deluded thoughts run on.

The crux of scattered-mind Buddha-recitation is this: can a practice that runs counter to the Buddha's teaching and to the instructions of the patriarchs ever achieve ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death? And ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death are the condition for rebirth
(for details, see
The Conditions for Rebirth
On this point,
Great Master Daochuo long ago gave a clear teaching:
"The wise diligently gather in the mind
(reciting the Buddha's name single-mindedly in daily life)
, and at the end of life the mind is not scattered;
one who does not train the mind to concentrate
(who recites with a scattered mind in daily life)
will surely be scattered at the end of life
(For details, see
Great Master Daochuo's Instructions on Pure Practice
Great Master Yongming, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
The present is the cause, and the time of death is the fruit. The cause must be genuine, and then the fruit will not be false.
If you wish
to accomplish the ten thoughts at the moment of death,
then prepare the ford and the bridge in advance
(that is, make full preparation beforehand)
, gather your merits and dedicate them to that hour
(dedicate them to the moment of death)
so that not a single thought is wanting, and then you need have no worry."

(Collection of Myriad Good Deeds Returning to the One) Therefore the likelihood that one who recites with a scattered mind will be reborn is exceedingly small, and it is not the case that such a person "is certain to be reborn as well." Those who recite the Buddha's name must be on their guard

The great harm of championing the ideas that "calling the name guarantees rebirth," that "scattered-mind Buddha-recitation is also certain to bring rebirth," and that "faith and vows alone are also certain to bring rebirth" lies in this: they mislead students onto a wrong path, so that not only is this life wasted, but wrong views are planted in the ālaya-consciousness and exert a latent influence through life after life to come:
"They delight in inferior teachings; within right view they give rise to the notion of wrong view, and within wrong view they give rise to the notion of right view."
(Sutra of the Buddha's Treasury)

Look closely at those for whom right Dharma and right view grate on the ear, while they warmly embrace wrong Dharma and wrong views, and you will know how terrifying this latent influence, this karmic force, can be: from delusion into delusion, they set out on a road of no return. Hence the ancients said:
"Better a thousand years without awakening than a single day on the wrong road."
Conversely, when one guides students by the right Dharma of
"right mindfulness at the moment of death, and the Buddha responds and comes to welcome,"
"ten thoughts at the moment of death, continued and one is reborn,"
"ten continuous thoughts made a settled habit,"
and
"if one can keep thought following thought without interruption, making this a lifetime commitment, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn,"

then they can put an end to birth and death in this very life; and even if in this life they do not achieve ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death, right view has been planted in the ālaya-consciousness and will blossom and bear fruit in lives to come.
[Original text] Great Master Hanshan's Song of Wasted Leisure says: "Reciting the Buddha's name is easy; to keep true faith is hard. When mind and mouth are not one, the labor all is marred
; the mouth recites Amitābha while the mind goes astray
(Note: the original reads "the mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is scattered"; for details, see
Great Master Hanshan: Song of Wasted Leisure (with Commentary)
, and though you shout your throat to bursting, it is all thrown away."

Some people are always doubtful: it is stressed that only single-minded Buddha-recitation can bring rebirth, and that those who recite with a scattered mind have no share in it. Is this claim correct? Let us consider it briefly below.
Commentary]
I now transcribe this teaching of Great Master Hanshan and annotate it as follows:

"To name the Buddha is easy; to keep true faith is hard. When mind and mouth are not one, the labor all is marred. The mouth recites Amitābha while the mind goes astray; though you shout your throat to bursting, it is all thrown away."

Translation: Reciting the Buddha's name is easy, but a sincere and truthful mind is hard. When mind and mouth are not one (the mind is not sincere and truthful: the mouth recites the Buddha's name while the mind dwells on other things), all is idle (all is wasted effort); the mouth recites Amitābha while the mind dwells on other things, and though the throat is shouted hoarse, it is all in vain.

[Faith] A sincere and truthful mind; when mind and mouth are not one, it is false. Hence the next line reads, "when mind and mouth are not one, the labor all is marred." [Sincere and truthful] Honest, not deceptive.
Great Master Hanshan's
"the mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is scattered; though you shout your throat to bursting, it is all in vain"
— this teaching
is the blood-and-tears lesson about scattered-mind Buddha-recitation that a thousand years of experience have proven

, and so Great Master Hanshan, thoroughly versed in both Chan and Pure Land, earnestly warned those who recite the Buddha's name in his Song of Wasted Leisure. For example, the essay Getting the Conditions for Rebirth Straight says: "Recently someone told me, very tense and heavy-hearted, that the head of a certain large chanting-assistance group in Taiwan had a very poor death and did not attain rebirth in the West. Others, greatly discouraged, said that a certain Master had bowed to the Buddha two and a half million times, yet his death was also poor, and he too probably did not attain rebirth in the West." Are such lessons not painful enough? As for the reasoning and evidence that scattered-mind recitation does not assure rebirth, see
Is Scattered-Mind Buddha-Recitation Also Certain to Bring Rebirth?

[Great Master Hanshan, thoroughly versed in both Chan and Pure Land] In order to bring students of the Dharma to liberation from birth and death in this very life, Great Master Hanshan pointed everywhere to the Pure Land and spent his whole life advocating and spreading the Pure Land method, perfect and clear in both principle and practice. He also led by example, seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and achieved splendid results (see the Record of Pure Land Sages). Moreover, because his former vow had not yet been fulfilled, he appeared again in this world as Great Master Xingce, the tenth patriarch of the Pure Land school. Great Master Yinguang praised him thus:
"Hanshan's ancient vow was not yet fulfilled, and so he appeared again as Jieliu
(Great Master Xingce)
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang:
"The Tenth Pure Land Patriarch of the Qing: Great Master Xingce of Puren Monastery, Yushan"
) (for details, see
Chan and Pure Land Master: Great Master Hanshan
[Original text] The very substance of ordinary beings is nothing but deluded thought, like a clay figure: even ground down to the very last speck of dust, it is still clay.
[Commentary]
If that is so, then tell me:
where is the
buddha-nature that ordinary beings share equally with all Buddhas?
Where do the three trainings of the Dharma — precepts, samādhi, and prajñā — come from? Apart from precepts, samādhi, and prajñā, is it still the Dharma?
The Original Vow teaching destroys the whole Dharma at its root by denying precepts, denying samādhi, and denying prajñā!)

In fact, it is not that ordinary beings are incapable of being free of deluded thoughts; the key is to find the method that stills deluded thoughts and to train oneself according to that correct method. This is what it means to practice with both feet firmly on the ground. Thus the scriptures and treatises all say: "Focus the mind on one point, and there is nothing that cannot be accomplished." How, then, are deluded thoughts to be stilled?
Awareness in Buddha-Recitation
explains this in detail.

I heard of an old woman who, because deluded thoughts would not stop while she recited the Buddha's name, grew so furious that she banged her head against the wall, saying as she banged, "Take that, deluded thoughts! Take that, deluded thoughts!" When someone asked her, "And after all that banging, what then?" she said, "The deluded thoughts still will not stop." One cannot help but sigh. Had someone with clear eyes told her how to still deluded thoughts, would she have come to this?
So it is not that many who recite the Buddha's name are not diligent, or not strenuous, but that they have not found the correct way to recite
[Original text] Moreover, when the body is drowning in the evil world of the five turbidities and the land is impure, how can the mind be pure?

[Commentary] Śākyamuni Buddha taught and expounded the Dharma for forty-nine years precisely to teach sentient beings how to cultivate a pure mind amid the evil world of the five turbidities. The patriarchs and great masters of every generation, and the reciters recorded in the biographies of the reborn, all attained a pure mind without exception! Those whose attainment of a pure mind was never recorded, reciters and Chan practitioners alike, are beyond counting. Great Master Huiyuan formed a society at Mount Lu to recite the Buddha's name; all one hundred and twenty-three of its members attained rebirth, and each of them showed auspicious signs of rebirth. This is clear proof.

Thoughts are of three kinds: coarse thoughts, subtle thoughts, and exceedingly subtle thoughts. For one who recites the Buddha's name, for example, deluded thoughts are coarse thoughts, and the thought of the Buddha-recitation is a subtle thought. Exceedingly subtle thoughts are the minute arising and ceasing, the flow and change, of the discriminating mind, and are the mark of the ālaya-consciousness. Accordingly, the pure mind has several corresponding levels: coarse thoughts stilled, subtle thoughts stilled, exceedingly subtle thoughts temporarily stilled, and exceedingly subtle thoughts stilled forever. When coarse thoughts are stilled, that is single-mindedness (the ten thousand thoughts returning to one). Going further, when subtle thoughts are stilled, that is what is commonly called no-thought (the one returning to nothing). For example, when Elder Master Xuyun described the eve of his awakening to the mind and seeing the nature, he was in the state of no-thought:

"The officers of the meditation hall would not assign me a rotation of duty, so I had the leisure to practice. From then on the ten thousand thoughts suddenly ceased; my practice settled into place, and night and day were as one."

(The Autobiographical Chronicle of Elder Master Xuyun) Going further still, when exceedingly subtle thoughts are temporarily stilled, that is the Chan state of awakening to the mind and seeing the nature (seeing one's original face thoroughly). If exceedingly subtle thoughts are stilled forever, that is Buddhahood.

For one who recites the Buddha's name, attaining single-mindedness (the stilling of coarse thoughts) is the most reliable guarantee of rebirth, and so practitioners of old laid great stress on raising a single thought alone and on practicing in accord with the single-mindedness described in the Buddha Speaks of Amitābha Sutra. Since the minimum requirement for rebirth is:
ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death
(for details, see
Amitābha's Original Vow
Therefore Great Masters Tanluan, Daochuo, and Shandao, out of great compassion, earnestly taught those who recite the Buddha's name to bring ten continuous thoughts to the point of becoming
a settled habit
, so as to ensure ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death and rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. (For details, see
Great Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teachings
Great Master Daochuo's Instructions on Pure Practice
, and
Great Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
[Original text]
Can a brick be polished into a mirror? How can iron sand be refined out of wood?
[Commentary]

Chan often says, "Polishing a brick cannot make a mirror," meaning: if the path of practice itself is wrong, how can one realize the fruit? So if Buddha-recitation is to bring rebirth, it must be done in the correct way. This is why Great Master Hanshan earnestly warned:
"The mouth recites Amitābha while the mind is scattered; though you shout your throat to bursting, it is all in vain."
For

polishing a brick cannot make a mirror (if the method of recitation itself is wrong, how can one attain rebirth?). But polishing copper can make a mirror, and so Great Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
"Continued, and one is reborn."

We must recite the Buddha's name in accordance with the scriptures and with the instructions of the patriarchs and great masters, so as to ensure our rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[Polishing a brick cannot make a mirror] This is what Mazu used to awaken Chan Master Huairang. (For the story, see the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp.)
[Original text] The wise will understand
every movement of an ordinary being's mind is a deluded mind. May I ask, how many people ever reach single-minded Buddha-recitation?
The Buddha must surely know of this. Otherwise, would not those who recite with a scattered mind be abandoned by the Buddha and left unsaved?
[Commentary]

Since ancient times, those who recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly have been too many to enumerate; one need only read the biographies of the reborn, ancient and modern, to know this. It is not that the Buddha abandons scattered-mind reciters and does not save them; rather, they do not practice in accord with the Buddha's teaching as it was spoken, and so they abandon the Buddha themselves.

[Original text] Reciting the Buddha's name truly is easy, but to believe and accept the principle of Amitābha's deliverance, that truly is hard to believe. I always thought that only when one had exerted oneself in recitation until the mind became pure could one be born in the Pure Land; only then would Amitābha appreciate us and guide us to rebirth. That is to plant a knife in the Buddha's heart, and it truly grieves one.
[Commentary] The "principle of Amitābha's deliverance"
is this:
Right mindfulness at the moment of death, and the Buddha responds and comes to welcome.
For details, see
The Principle of Rebirth
Reciting the Buddha's name until the mind becomes pure —

only then is one attuned to the Pure Land, only then does one resonate with Amitābha Buddha, who comes to guide one onward. This is what the Buddha taught in many sutras; it is not "planting a knife in the Buddha's heart."

[Original text] It has been ten kalpas since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood. Every day he longs for us, straining his eyes, to recite the Buddha's name and be reborn in the Pure Land; the Buddha always stands waiting for us, pulling us back from falling into hell. The scriptures always say: only by reciting the Buddha's name can one attain rebirth; never do they say that one must cultivate to the point of a pure mind before one can be reborn, or that a scattered mind cannot attain rebirth. Therefore we should know that rebirth depends entirely on Amitābha's deliverance and does not depend on the depth of an ordinary being's skill in recitation! Rebirth is determined solely by whether the practitioner has faith and vows.

[Commentary] "Rebirth depends entirely on Amitābha's deliverance" — this is correct. If there were no deliverance by Amitābha Buddha, then for sentient beings to put an end to birth and death they would have to cut off every trace of view-afflictions and thought-afflictions, a task whose difficulty exceeds rebirth through Buddha-recitation by more times than can be counted! As for the reasoning and evidence that "a scattered mind cannot attain rebirth," see
Is Scattered-Mind Buddha-Recitation Also Certain to Bring Rebirth?

Rebirth is determined solely by whether the practitioner has faith and vows" — this wrongly erases practice from the three provisions of faith, vows, and practice. Faith and vows that have lost practice are hollow faith and floating vows that never touch the ground. One who recites the Buddha's name must be clear about the conditions for rebirth and about the relationship among faith, vows, and practice; otherwise one will ruin the great matter of rebirth and miss the precious opportunity. As for the conditions for rebirth, see
The Conditions for Rebirth
. As for the relationship among faith, vows, and practice, see
Faith, Vows, and Practice

[The three provisions of faith, vows, and practice] Provisions are like those for a long journey: one needs funds, and one needs food. Lacking these two things, one can never arrive. Pure Land practice is likewise a long journey: only with all three, faith, vows, and practice, can one reach the destination.
These three provisions of faith, vows, and practice are the heart of Pure Land practice. The three are inseparable, and their relationship is this:
Faith awakens vows, vows guide practice; practice fulfills vows, practice confirms faith.

These sixteen characters are the basic guideline of Pure Land practice. That is to say, faith and vows must be grounded in practice to be true faith and earnest vows; and practice is the actual deed that confirms faith and fulfills vows, as well as the measure by which one tests how true one's faith and how earnest one's vows are. One who recites the Buddha's name must have true faith and earnest vows, and must practice according to the scriptural texts, just as they were spoken.
Great Master Yinguang taught:

"Since you have true faith and earnest vows, you should cultivate the primary practice of Buddha-recitation. Take faith and vows as the guide and Buddha-recitation as the primary practice. Faith, vows, and practice, these three are the essential principle of the Buddha-recitation method. With practice but without faith and vows, one cannot attain rebirth; with faith and vows but without practice, one likewise cannot attain rebirth. When faith, vows, and practice are all complete and lacking nothing, rebirth is certain."
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang:
"A Letter to Upasaka Chen Xizhou"
The reason Buddha-recitation requires single-mindedness (a pure mind) is that
"by the pure mind of Buddha-recitation, one resonates into rebirth in the Western Pure Land"
— this is the principle by which recitation brings rebirth. Great Master Yinguang taught:

"Only where there is a Pure Land of the mind can one be born in the Western Pure Land. If one's own mind is impure, how can one attain rebirth at once? Even when a sinner of the five heinous crimes and the ten evils attains rebirth through ten recitations, it is by the pure mind of Buddha-recitation that he
resonates into rebirth in the
Western Pure Land."
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang:
"Twenty-seven Answers to Upasaka Qu Tianxiang's Questions"
) He also said:
"To recite the Buddha's name with a scattered mind, it is hard to attain rebirth."
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang:
"A Letter to Upasaka Chen Xizhou"

[Original text] Those who recite with a scattered mind are also among the sentient beings of the ten directions! If even flying insects and wriggling worms can attain rebirth, why can those who recite with a scattered mind not attain rebirth? Compassionate Amitābha Buddha would never set up a high threshold as a condition for rebirth.
[Commentary] That even flying insects and wriggling worms can attain rebirth

is because they practiced as it was spoken. Master Tanxu's Recollections of Dust and Shadows in the Mind tells the story of a rooster's rebirth: "When Master Dixian was at Toutuo Monastery in Wenzhou, there was a large rooster that followed the assembly in reciting the Buddha's name every day. One day, when the recitation was finished, the rooster still would not leave the Buddha hall, and the incense-and-lamp keeper, about to close the doors, shooed it away. It ran to the center of the great hall, faced the Buddha image, crowed three times, and died standing. The old master treated it as he would a monk, cremating it and burying it behind the mountain. That rooster must have been a monk in a former life, and his practice must have been quite good; at the moment of death a single mistaken thought turned him into an animal body, yet he still had spiritual awareness and knew to recite the Buddha's name." This rooster's rebirth was also because he practiced as it was spoken; therefore it cannot prove that one who recites with a scattered mind is certain to attain rebirth.

Right mindfulness at the moment of death is by no means a high threshold set up by Amitābha Buddha; rather, at the crucial moment of choosing where to go, it is you yourself who decide where you will go.
Will you drift away amid deluded thoughts, following your karma, or keep right mindfulness and move the Buddha to come and welcome you?

[Original text] So everyone should listen to what the Buddha said, and not traffic in hearsay and thereby swell their own ignorance. Do as the Buddhist scriptures say. Looking in turn at the many schools of exposition in this age of the Dharma's decline, are they truly pure and orthodox Pure Land thought?
[Commentary] "Do as the Buddhist scriptures say" — how right this saying is! This is what is meant by
practicing as it was spoken
. Read the Sutra of Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha's Sustaining Power, and you will see how the Buddha taught us over and over:
practice as it was spoken, and attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
(For details, see
A Commentary on the Sutra of Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha's Sustaining Power

) As for the many schools of exposition in the age of the Dharma's decline, one must see whether they accord with the scriptures and treatises and with the instructions of the Pure Land patriarchs through the generations. Whatever does not accord, or distorts, or tears passages from their context, is erroneous and heterodox. Whatever fully accords is pure and orthodox Pure Land thought and should be followed and put into practice. For example, both Great Master Tanluan and Great Master Daochuo taught:
Ten thoughts at the moment of death, continued, and one is reborn.
And to achieve ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death, one must in daily life achieve:
ten continuous thoughts made a settled habit.
(For details, see
Great Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teachings
Great Master Daochuo's Instructions on Pure Practice
, and
Ten Thoughts at the Moment of Death: Continued, and One Is Reborn
) Thus Great Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
"Precisely because calling the name is easy
(because reciting the name is easier than visualization-recitation)
, one is reborn as soon as the recitation continues unbroken
(at the moment of death, provided that the thought of Buddha-recitation continues without being interrupted by deluded thoughts, one attains rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
. If one can keep thought following thought without interruption, making this a lifetime commitment,
(one who practices thus for the whole of this life)
, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn."
(For details, see
Great Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching

.) Why not follow it and put it into practice? Why refuse to heed the words of the patriarchs and the words of Amitābha Buddha, and instead believe the erroneous notion that "scattered-mind Buddha-recitation is also certain to bring rebirth"?
[Making it a settled habit] Through constant, repeated practice, ten continuous thoughts become second nature.
[The erroneous notion that "scattered-mind Buddha-recitation is also certain to bring rebirth"] For details, see
Refuting "Scattered-Mind Buddha-Recitation Is Also Certain to Bring Rebirth"

Pay special attention to this: the Original Vow teaching, and figures of that stripe such as Master Huijing and Master Jingzong, revere Great Masters Tanluan, Daochuo, and Shandao as patriarchs, yet they never teach their followers these extremely important instructions of the patriarchs:

"Ten thoughts at the moment of death, continued, and one is reborn." "Ten continuous thoughts made a settled habit." "If one can keep thought following thought without interruption, making this a lifetime commitment, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn."

Instead they set themselves squarely against the patriarchs and loudly champion the erroneous notions that "calling the name guarantees rebirth" and that "scattered-mind Buddha-recitation is also certain to bring rebirth"

[Original text] The purpose of Buddha-recitation is to fulfill the Buddha's vow; one who rides the Buddha's vow will surely attain rebirth. The purpose of recitation is not a pure mind, and a pure mind cannot be made the condition for rebirth. The Buddha cares only whether you recite the Buddha's name; he truly does not care whether you are single-minded or scattered. Chan is far too profound for people of our capacity to reach. We ordinary beings should simply keep to a simple-minded recitation and not add our own reasoning. Rebirth is accomplished by the inconceivable power of merit of the Buddha's name. Recitation is up to me; the welcoming is up to the Buddha. There is no time even for recitation, so do not go picking fault for no reason, forever doubting and suspecting in the matter of scattered-mind recitation not bringing rebirth.
[Commentary] "The purpose of Buddha-recitation is to fulfill the Buddha's vow; one who rides the Buddha's vow will surely attain rebirth." —
The eighteenth vow is Amitābha Buddha's original vow.
As for the meaning of the eighteenth vow, Great Master Daochuo clearly taught in the Collection of Peace and Bliss:
"If there are sentient beings who, though they have committed evil their whole lives,
at the end of their lives, with ten continuous thoughts, call my name,
and if they are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Here Great Master Daochuo gives a precise explanation of the meaning of "even to ten thoughts" in the eighteenth vow:
At the end of life, with ten continuous thoughts, calling my name.
Therefore in daily practice one must earnestly make ten continuous thoughts a settled habit, so as to ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. (For details, see
The Eighteenth Vow
Ten Thoughts at the Moment of Death: Continued, and One Is Reborn
) As for the
conditions for rebirth, what then are they?
The conditions for rebirth are:
ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death.
That is to say,

provided that at the moment of death the thought of Buddha-recitation continues for ten thoughts without being interrupted by deluded thoughts, one resonates with Amitābha Buddha and is guided by the Buddha to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
For details, see
The Conditions for Rebirth
. Therefore both Great Master Tanluan and Great Master Daochuo taught:
Ten continuous thoughts at the point of death, and rebirth is attained.
(For details, see
Great Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teachings
Great Master Daochuo's Instructions on Pure Practice
Spiritual response and communion: the subjective influence of sentient beings and the response of Amitābha Buddha mutually reach and interpenetrate each other.
The original says:
The recitation rests on me; the welcoming and guidance rest on the Buddha.
The answer is: therefore when I recite, I must be in spiritual response and communion with the Buddha, so as to receive the Buddha's welcome and guidance.
The original says:
“Do not go finding fault for no reason, forever suspecting and fretting over this matter of whether scattered-mind recitation can attain rebirth.”

The answer is: whether a path can lead to rebirth is a matter of the greatest importance! If you do not get it clear and are dragged confused into the fire pit, to gain a human body again, to hear the Dharma again, to cultivate the Pure Land again — who knows which eon and which life that will be! Do you still wish to suffer in this endless long night, with unremitting pain and torment? And when that time comes, whom will you blame?

[Original]Scattered-mind recitation is quite normal; precisely because there are deluded thoughts, one recites. For one who constantly calls the Buddha's name, scattering naturally stills, the deluded mind naturally ceases, the three karmas naturally harmonize, and the vow-mind naturally arises. No one lives out a hundred years, yet all harbor a thousand years of worry. Scattered-mind recitation is still better than none at all; but to be able to recite with a focused mind is of course even better.

The universal path, in order to end birth and death and escape transmigration, must pass through the myriad thoughts returning to one, the one returning to nothing, the illumination of the mind and seeing of one's own nature, then the practice of maintaining, until the delusions of views and thought are cut off entirely; only then can one end birth and death and escape transmigration. Therefore
a focused, undisturbed mind (
the myriad thoughts returning to one
) is but the initial stage of practice; as long as the method is correct and one
diligently and untiringly
works at it, everyone can reach it.

Hence the saying: of ten thousand who cultivate, ten thousand go. The key of “of ten thousand who cultivate, ten thousand go” lies in cultivating — cultivating correctly, cultivating diligently and untiringly!

In fact, a focused, undisturbed mind is not beyond reach. From ancient times on through the Ming and Qing dynasties, Buddhism in China was mainly Chan; therefore many Chan practitioners wrongly held that reciting with a focused, undisturbed mind to attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land is an expedient method set up for people of dull faculties. And many of those who cultivated the Pure Land practiced mainly the samādhi of Buddha-recitation and the pratyutpanna samādhi, so a focused, undisturbed mind was nothing worth mentioning. How is it that now a focused, undisturbed mind is spoken of as high above the clouds and looked on as a fearful path? In the sutras, treatises, and the records and sayings of the Chan school, there are countless methods and instances of reaching the myriad thoughts returning to one and focusing the mind on a single point; why not study and practice them? Why belittle oneself, declaring oneself good for nothing, and even casting away one's own Buddha-nature, identical to that of all Buddhas? For example, the original says:

“Ordinary beings are in their substance entirely deluded thought, like a clay statue of a man; even ground down to the last grain, it is still clay. How much more so when the body is sunk in the five turbid worlds and the land is impure — how can the mind be pure? Can grinding a brick make a mirror? How can iron ore be refined out of wood?”

Cultivating the samādhi of Buddha-recitation: cultivating the samādhi of Buddha-recitation is mindful holding through principle, reciting the Buddha of one's own nature (the Amitābha of one's own nature) to see through to the original face. The eighth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Lianchi (Zhuhong), says:

“Know that the Pure Land is mind-only; there is no external realm.” “In accord with principle, then one's own nature returns to the original substance; this is the meaning of vowing to be born in that land.” “Reciting the Buddha is reciting the mind; being born there does not depart from being born here. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are one substance, abiding neither on the middle current nor on either shore. Hence it is called the Amitābha of one's own nature, the mind-only Pure Land.”

(The Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra). The pratyutpanna samādhi, also called the samādhi of the Buddha standing, means that the one who cultivates this samādhi and attains accomplishment can see the Buddhas of the ten directions standing before him. In practice, one neither sits nor lies down, from morning to night and from night to morning, either walking or standing, taking ninety days as one period, and single-mindedly recites the name of Amitābha Buddha.

Answer: This is all the doing of Master Huijing of the Primal Vow Dharma-door
(for background on this person, see in detail
What Is the Primal Vow Dharma-door?

The term Pure Land school originally referred to the sect among the ten schools of Buddhism that specializes in reciting the Buddha to seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, with Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty as its first patriarch,
a great sect standing side by side with the Chan school for a thousand years

. Yet their Primal Vow Dharma-door is but a small school, and Master Huijing actually names it the “Pure Land school,” as though they were the entire Pure Land school! This is a deliberate creation of confusion, passing off fish eyes as pearls and the false for the true, so as to deceive those who do not know the facts — especially beginning students of Buddhism — into mistakenly thinking they are the Pure Land school and boarding a pirate ship. — This is the means by which the Primal Vow Dharma-door survives:
deception!
Buddhist disciples must open their eyes wide,

and whenever they encounter those organizations and websites that take the name “Pure Land school,” they must carefully distinguish whether or not it is the Primal Vow Dharma-door, so as not to be taken in

. The way to distinguish them is also simple: if it is led by Master Huijing, Master Jingzong, and others, advocating the views and theories of the Primal Vow Dharma-door — for example the Pure Land school Hongyuan Temple, the Pure Land school
Pure Land school Portal

Global Pure Land school Portal Website, the Chinese Pure Land school Association — these are the Primal Vow Dharma-door that attaches itself to Buddhism as an external way, and not the true Pure Land school,
their true name should be: the Primal Vow Dharma-door Hongyuan Temple, the China Primal Vow Dharma-door
Global Portal Website, the Chinese Primal Vow Dharma-door Association, and the like; only then would name and reality correspond
